question: A 20-year-old man from Assam presents with his third episode of meningococcal meningitis in 5 years. Investigations reveal a specific complement deficiency. Which complement component is most likely deficient?

answers.text: C5 or a later terminal complement component (C5–C9)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Terminal complement components C5–C9 form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC), which lyses Gram-negative bacteria by inserting a transmembrane pore. Neisseria meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae are uniquely dependent on MAC for immune clearance. Deficiency of any terminal component predisposes specifically to recurrent Neisseria infections.

Incorrect. C1q deficiency is associated with SLE-like autoimmune disease due to impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris, not recurrent Neisseria meningitis. Recurrent meningococcal infections point to terminal complement (C5–C9) deficiency affecting the Membrane Attack Complex.

Incorrect. C3 is the convergence point of all three activation pathways; its deficiency causes broad susceptibility to pyogenic bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, S. aureus), not specifically Neisseria. The pattern of recurrent meningococcal disease specifically implicates terminal complement (C5–C9) and the MAC.

Incorrect. C4 deficiency affects the classical and lectin pathways and is associated with SLE-like disease and increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria generally. The specific pattern of recurrent Neisseria meningitis implicates terminal complement components (C5–C9), which form the MAC required for Neisseria clearance.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the three activation pathways converge at C3 → C5, leading to MAC (C5b–C9) formation. MAC deficiency specifically predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.
Excellent! Recurrent Neisseria infections are the hallmark of terminal complement (MAC) deficiency — a high-yield clinical association.
